pr_title: [POC] apply explicit SELinux label on tempfile in copy
pr_body:
##### SUMMARY
fixes #80269 

SELinux labels are only applied at the final stage of the `copy` module, however, the system policy may require a specific context for the file accessed by the process in the `validate` step, which will not be present on the intermediate tempfile that validate is run against. This change applies explicitly-set SELinux labels (including `_default` to use the policy default) to the tempfile when `validate` is used (consistent with the other permissions/ownership things we were already doing).

##### ISSUE TYPE
<!--- Pick one below and delete the rest -->
- Bugfix Pull Request

##### COMPONENT NAME
copy.py

issue_context.title: template validation fails because of SELinux errors
issue_context.body:
### Summary

I am using the [nsenter connection plugin](https://docs.ansible.com/ansible/latest/collections/community/docker/nsenter_connection.html) to run Ansible in a privileged podman container against the local host.
I want to use a template to write a /etc/sysconfig/iptables file, and use `/usr/sbin/iptables-restore` for template validation to avoid accidentally writing invalid iptables rules. This causes a SELinux violation, I believe because the template validation is performed on a file in `/root/.ansible` with SELinux label "unconfined_u:object_r:admin_home_t:s0".  It seems like the correct SELinux label would be applied only after the template validation, when the file is placed in /etc/sysconfig/iptables (or perhaps more accurately, the existing label of the destination file would be used and Ansible would not change it).

It seems to me that Ansible should perform the template validation on the source file using the SELinux labels that the destination file would have, to avoid general problems with validation commands being denied by SELinux.

Update: the default SELinux rules block it due to the SELinux type of the process in the container, not the type of the template file. Nevertheless SELinux may block different things for different reasons and a handle to adjust the SELinux label of the template file before validation rather than after could be a versatile way to avoid such issues, and in general it may be possible to avoid a SELinux denial by either changing the process type or file type.

### Issue Type

Bug Report

### Component Name

ansible.builtin.template

### Ansible Version

### OS / Environment

Fresh CentOS8 Stream VM with latest updates as of Mar 21.
Then in a Fedora 36 podman pod, I install and run Ansible.

Playbook in the pod is play.yml :
```
- hosts: testhost
  connection: community.docker.nsenter
  tasks:
    - name: Test
      template:
        src: template.j2
        dest: /etc/sysconfig/iptables
        owner: "root"
        group: "root"
        mode: "0600"
        validate: "/usr/sbin/iptables-restore --test %s"
#     Setting seuser, setype don't help
#       seuser: system_u
#       setype: etc_t
```

### Steps to Reproduce

On CentOS8 Stream:
```
sudo dnf -y install podman
sudo podman run --pull=newer --rm -it --pid=host --privileged fedora:36
# inside the pod
dnf -y install ansible
echo testhost >> /etc/ansible/hosts
echo whatevs >> template.j2
ansible-playbook play.yml --diff -vvv
```

### Expected Results

The source file that the template validation command is executed on should have an appropriate SELinux label (for example that of the destination file) , allowing the template validation command to run on it just as it would on the destination file. 

Failing that I should be able to control the SELinux label of the source file _before_ the validation command is run on it using e.g. the `setype` option of the template module, but this does not work either. It only seems to be applied to the final destination file after template validation.


This shows that the source file (`/root/.ansible/tmp/ansible-tmp-1679434955.1837838-7840-193608485627336/source`) that the template validation is running on has the SELinux label "unconfined_u:object_r:admin_home_t:s0" which is not appropriate for a system config file. If it was instead e.g. "system_u:object_r:system_conf_t:s0" then the iptables-restore command would be able to run on it.

Perhaps this kind of issue is only exposed when using the nsenter connection plugin?

Yeah, more than likely it's something specific to the nsenter connection; typically a full container runtime will properly interact with the system SELinux policy to Do The Right Thing for mapping this stuff, but I don't think nsenter has any of that logic in place... You might want to consider if there's a way to do what you want under an actual container runtime, or work with the owners of nsenter to see if they can get the system container policies to apply under its context.

It's unlikely there's anything that can be done in ansible-core itself to address this, so we're going to close this issue.

(moving discussion back here from https://github.com/ansible-collections/community.docker/issues/599)

In response to discussion at https://github.com/ansible-collections/community.docker/issues/599#issuecomment-1482060763:

If I had to guess, the system policy is applying another dimension to the process and/or filesystem contexts involving the container namespace... But again we're exceeding my depth of knowledge about how SELinux actually works in containers :wink: .

Explicitly labeling the tempfile the same way the final file would be labeled when the SELinux args are specified does seem like a decent compromise off the top of my head... The difference in filesystem location *shouldn't* trip any different policies than it would in the final location from Ansible's perspective if the label's the same- if the system policy lets us hack on the final file, it should let us do the same to the relabeled tempfile, and if not, it's going to fail later anyway when it goes to touch the destination file. The only (possibly) remaining issue I can think of then would just be ensuring that the policy allows Ansible itself to write to the destination, which you'd have to have working regardless.

I've reopened this issue while we explore this idea...

@rptaylor do you know how to run Ansible from source? If so, give https://github.com/ansible/ansible/pull/80302 a try and see if it fixes your issue; you'd need to pass an explicit value or  `_default` for `serole`/`seuser`/`setype` along with your `validate` to trigger the new behavior.

Thanks @nitzmahone ! 

When I did further testing yesterday https://github.com/ansible-collections/community.docker/issues/599#issuecomment-1482060763 , I noticed that the label of a pre-validation template file is actually always "unconfined_u:object_r:admin_home_t:s0" whether you're in a container or not (as long as you're root it writes in /root/.ansible), and it works normally but not from podman/nsenter, which implies the problem is the source label of the iptables-restore process (which I am not sure how to debug), not the target label of the template file.  So my initial impression of the problem was a bit off, sorry.

Hmmm, nevertheless, it looks like there might be a rule that would allow the file to be read by an iptables_t process if the file had the "usual" system_conf_t label:
```
[centos@centos8 ~]$ sudo sesearch -A -s iptables_t -c file -p read | grep system_conf
allow iptables_t system_conf_t:file { append create getattr ioctl link lock open read rename setattr unlink write };
```
so the goal of providing a handle to workaround SELinux quirks is still valid I think and would be worth a try.

 I'm not familiar with compiling or running Ansible from source, are there some docs for that?

It's pretty easy- just do something like:

```
python3 -m pip install https://github.com/nitzmahone/ansible/archive/refs/heads/tempfile_secontext.tar.gz

ansible --version
```

and verify from the version output that you're running an unreleased ansible-core 2.15.0.dev0
(that command will install the archive from this PR branch)
(you also might want to uninstall the OS-packaged ansible while you're playing with this; this process shouldn't trash it, but depending on your PATH, you might pick up the wrong one)

Aha, when I add the template options
```
        seuser: system_u
        setype: system_conf_t
```
to the playbook and run that ansible build in a venv in podman, it works! There are no SELinux denials.

I also found [another workaround](https://github.com/containers/container-selinux/issues/221#issuecomment-1483800939) based on changing the SELinux type of the process in the container.

Is that with the fix in #80302, or just using an as-released ansible-core? At a glance, I don't see how explicitly setting the SELinux labeling should fix anything for `validate` (in the as-released code), since the labels appear to only be applied *after* the validation (which is what that PR changes). It's also entirely possible I'm missing something sneaky- the `template` action plugin dance is one of the most complex ones in core.

Yes, by "that build" I meant the instructions you provided to build:
 `python3 -m pip install https://github.com/nitzmahone/ansible/archive/refs/heads/tempfile_secontext.tar.gz`
Ah sorry, I missed that nuance. OK, cool- I'll move forward with cleaning up that PR for release then. Thanks for the validation!

@rptaylor also, could I trouble you to try it by setting all of `se(user|role|type)` to `_default` and see if it still works? Assuming the final destination file's labeling matches what it would be after a `restorecon` (which is what we're consulting to get the default values we'd apply)- that *should* also work, which has the added benefit of you not needing to hardcode details about the default system labels into your playbook, merely that you want it to be what the system thinks it should by the time we're all done.

Thanks!

Okay that's handy. I used
```
- hosts: testhost
  connection: community.docker.nsenter
  tasks:
    - name: Test
      template:
        src: template.j2
        dest: /etc/sysconfig/iptables2
        owner: "root"
        group: "root"
        mode: "0600"
        validate: "/usr/sbin/iptables-restore --test %s"
        seuser: _default
        serole: _default
        setype: _default
```

and it worked:
```
[centos@centos8 ~]$ ls -lZ /etc/sysconfig/iptables
-rw-------. 1 root root system_u:object_r:system_conf_t:s0 75 Mar 28 18:22 /etc/sysconfig/iptables
```
